descriptions: The Self realized by the renouncer as 'so'ham' — 'I am He' (Maitreya 2.1; Nāradaparivrājaka 9).
The sixteenth measure of the praṇava and the state beyond the fourth (Nāradaparivrājaka 8; Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka).
That in which renunciation consists: the union of jīva and the supreme (Maitreya 2.17).
negations: not reached by staff, shaving, garb or show (Nāradaparivrājaka 5)
relation_to_self: Identical: the renouncer's own Self is Brahman, and the jīva in the body-temple is Śiva alone (Maitreya 2.1; Avadhūta 1). In the Vaiṣṇava Śāṭyāyanīya the renouncer serves Viṣṇu and bears his marks.
relation_to_world: The world is renounced as the field of the three desires (for wife, wealth and worlds); for the knower it is superimposed and no longer binding; rites cease because 'the sun of consciousness neither rises nor sets' (Maitreya 2.14).
caveat: The renunciate ideal is a way of life before it is a doctrine: the texts insist that the ultimate is realized only by one who has actually abandoned the ritual world, and they disagree among themselves (Advaitin paramahaṃsa vs Vaiṣṇava tridaṇḍin) on whether outer marks are to be kept. A one-truth reading must not dissolve that insistence on renunciation or the Vaiṣṇava strand's theism.
